## Diagnosis

You were diagnosed with **acute appendicitis, non-perforated**. Appendicitis means the appendix is inflamed. The appendix is a small, tube-like organ attached to the first part of the large intestine, in the lower right part of the abdomen [2]. "Non-perforated" means, as written in your document, that it had not burst. Your document says no abscess (a pocket of infection) or free air was seen on the CT scan.

## Procedure

You had a **laparoscopic appendectomy** on 06/05/2026. This is surgery to remove the appendix using small cuts. Your document says there were 3 small incisions: at the belly button, the lower left abdomen, and just above the pubic bone.

- Anesthesia: General. Anesthesia is the use of medicines to prevent pain during surgery [3].
- Estimated blood loss: Minimal (<10 mL).

## Hospital course

- You came to the emergency department (ED) with 18 hours of pain. It started around the belly button and moved to the right lower abdomen. You also had nausea and poor appetite.
- Your temperature was 38.1 C.
- A CT scan (a detailed X-ray picture) of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast showed a dilated (widened) appendix measuring 11 mm with surrounding inflammation.
- Before surgery you got one dose of IV ceftriaxone 2 g and metronidazole 500 mg. These are antibiotics. No more antibiotics were needed after surgery.
- Surgery was uncomplicated and done the same day.
- At discharge you were eating a regular diet, walking, urinating normally, and your pain was controlled with oral medicines.
- The pathology report (lab study of the removed tissue) is still pending.

## Lab results

- **WBC (white blood count): 14.2 x10^3/uL.** This is **above** the typical adult range of 4.5-11.0. Your report did not list a range, so this range is a typical one and not from your report. White blood cells are part of your immune system [1]. A high count can happen with infection or tissue damage from surgery, among other causes [1]. Your document does not say what caused your result.

## Wound care

- Your incisions are closed with dissolvable stitches under the skin and skin glue. Do not pick at the glue. It will peel off on its own in 7-14 days.
- You may shower starting 06/06/2026. Let soapy water run over the incisions and pat dry.
- No tub baths, hot tubs, or swimming for 2 weeks.
- Mild bruising and shoulder pain (from the gas used during surgery) are normal for a few days.

## Activity

- Walk several times a day.
- Do not lift more than 10 lb (4.5 kg) or do strenuous exercise for 2 weeks (until 06/20/2026).
- No driving while taking oxycodone.
- You may return to desk work in 3-5 days as comfortable.

## Medications

1. **Acetaminophen 500 mg tablets**: take 2 tablets (1,000 mg) by mouth every 8 hours for 3 days, then as needed. Maximum 3,000 mg in 24 hours. It relieves mild to moderate pain and reduces fever [5].
2. **Ibuprofen 200 mg tablets**: take 3 tablets (600 mg) by mouth every 6 hours as needed, with food. Maximum 2,400 mg in 24 hours. It is an NSAID, a type of pain reliever [6].
3. **Oxycodone 5 mg tablet**: 1 tablet by mouth every 6 hours ONLY if needed for severe pain not relieved by #1 and #2. Quantity 6 tablets, no refills. It is an opioid (narcotic) pain medicine used for severe pain [7].
4. **Docusate sodium 100 mg** by mouth twice daily while taking oxycodone. It is a stool softener, which makes stools easier to pass [8].

## When to call or return to the ED

Call the surgery clinic or return to the ED for:

- Fever higher than 101.0 F (38.3 C) or shaking chills
- Increasing redness, warmth, swelling, or pus draining from an incision
- Belly pain that is getting worse instead of better, or a hard, swollen belly
- Vomiting or being unable to keep down liquids
- No bowel movement or gas for more than 3 days
- Calf pain or swelling, or sudden shortness of breath

## Follow-up

General Surgery Clinic, Dr. B. Sample, MD, on 06/19/2026 at 1:30 PM for a wound check and pathology review. Clinic phone: (555) 010-0142.

This is an educational explanation, not medical advice. Talk to your doctor or care team about what this means for you.

- **Type 1 diabetes mellitus (diagnosed at age 11).** With type 1 diabetes, the body makes little or no insulin. Insulin is a hormone that helps glucose move into cells to be used for energy [5].
- **Viral gastroenteritis (trigger).** This is inflammation of the lining of the stomach and intestines caused by a virus. Its main symptoms are vomiting and diarrhea [6]. Your document lists it as the trigger.
